text: Feedback. The professor gives feedback after every presentation.
Room for improvement. There is some room for improvement in the slides.
Concise. Your part was concise and clear.
Pace. Your pace was too fast at the end.
Eye contact. Your eye contact was much better today.
Filler words. Try to use fewer filler words.
Take on board. Thank you. I'll take that on board.
Spot on. The numbers were spot on.

Good morning, group four. Here is my feedback on yesterday's presentation. First, the good news. Your recommendation was clear, and the numbers were spot on. Mauricio, your part was concise, and your eye contact was much better than on Monday. Now, the room for improvement. The presentation was too long. You had fifteen minutes and you used twenty-two. The slides had too many words, and the pace at the end was too fast. We could not follow it. And you did not leave enough time for questions. For Friday, please cut five slides, and rehearse with a clock. You are good enough to be the best group in the class.

I was fifty-one years old, and I had never received real feedback in English. After my first presentation, a classmate from Germany said, your ideas are strong, but you speak too fast and you use too many filler words. I wanted to defend myself. Then I remembered my own team at the bank. When I give them feedback, I want them to listen, not to argue. So I said, thank you, I will take that on board. The next day, I spoke more slowly, and I stopped saying, you know, every ten seconds. It was not perfect, but it was clear enough. On the last day, the same classmate said, your pace was spot on. That was the best feedback of my year.
